newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan polls point to clear LDP election victory.
newsitem.headline: Japan polls point to clear LDP election victory.

text.p: Two major voter surveys showed on Tuesday that Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto could be heading for a clear victory in Japan's general elections that would put his party back in sole charge of government.

The findings, the first to suggest the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) would clinch a parliamentary majority in Sunday's vote, were applauded by the stock market as a sign of a return to stability after three years of coalition rule.

The pro-business LDP, the dominant party in post-war Japan, held power for almost four decades until it was ousted in 1993. It came back into government around a year later but only as a coalition partner.

The polls by leading business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun -- which covered 150,000 voters -- and by Kyodo news agency -- which sampled 384,000 people -- showed the LDP was likely to achieve a simple majority of 251 seats, and possibly more, in the 500-seat Lower House.

Previous polls had put the LDP in the lead but not by enough of a margin to rule alone. Both the nationwide polls were conducted last weekend. The Lower House is the decisive chamber in Japan's parliament.
"The LDP...has almost consolidated the 211 seats it holds at present and is building momentum to reach at least a majority of 251 seats," the Nihon Keizai said.
"The LDP is looking at a single-handed majority...taking full advantage of the single-seat system which favours big parties," Kyodo said.
The prospect of one-party government boosted the Tokyo stock market. The key Nikkei average jumped 1.91 percent, or 400.68 points, to close at 21,429.93, also helped by a rally on Wall Street.

"There is a feeling of relief in the market that the political scene is beginning to take shape, which means that policies to prop up the economy have a chance of being carried out relatively smoothly," said Yamaichi Securities general manager Tadahiro Kamogawa.

"It didn't have to be the LDP, it could have been any of the parties," Kamogawa added. "The market was satisfied just to know that the political situation is showing signs of stabilising with the emergence of at least one dominant party."
The LDP held 211 Lower House seats when parliament was dissolved last month. It ruled in coalition with the Socialists and the Sakigake Party, an LDP splinter group.

The poll found voters appeared to be turning against Japan's main opposition group, Shinshinto (the New Frontier Party), which the Nihon Keizai poll said would struggle to maintain its present number of 160 seats. The Kyodo survey said Shinshinto may even lose ground and end up with only 140 seats.
The Democratic Party, formed only last month by defectors from the two smaller parties that were in the ruling coalition, was doing well and could win 52 seats, the two polls said.

The October 20 vote will be the first under a new electoral system in which 300 Lower House members will be chosen in single-seat constituencies, while another 200 will be elected through proportional representation in 11 regional blocs.

If the polls prove accurate, it would be a victory for Hashimoto in his determination to stick with an unpopular plan to raise Japan's sales tax from three to five percent in April. Shinshinto has tried to woo voters with promises of a huge cut in income tax and a pledge to delay a rise in the sales tax.
Political analysts said the apparent late surge by the LDP indicated that the organisational strength of the party was still intact despite the past three years of turmoil.
They said voters might also be deciding that the time had come to return to undivided leadership to get the country's sluggish economic recovery onto a growth.
Shinshinto, a grouping of nine parties, was formed at the end of 1994 and has struggled for unity among its members.
